methods.label: Join the tangent-circle centers
methods.explanation:
The areas of the small circles are already known. We first find the large circle's radius by joining centers of tangent circles.

[Figure 1](figures/2019_AMC_10A_Q16_question_fig1.svg)

Let \(O\) be the center of the middle unit circle. The six unit circles touching it form a ring, and consecutive circles in this ring also touch. Centers of externally tangent unit circles are 2 units apart, so \(O\) and every consecutive pair of ring centers form an equilateral triangle of side 2. Their six angles at \(O\) are each \(60^\circ\).

Choose consecutive ring centers \(A,B\), and let \(T\) be the center of the outer unit circle touching both corresponding circles. Then
\[
OA=OB=AB=TA=TB=2.
\]
Thus \(OAB\) and \(TAB\) are equilateral triangles on opposite sides of \(AB\). If \(M\) is the midpoint of \(AB\), their altitudes lie on the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\), and \(AM=1\). Pythagoras gives
\[
OM=TM=\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt3,
\]
so \(OT=2\sqrt3\).

The same construction applies to each of the six outer unit circles. Consequently their centers all lie at distance \(2\sqrt3\) from \(O\), in six equally spaced directions. This also justifies the center of the large circle: all six outer unit circles are internally tangent to it, so its center is equidistant from their centers. Three noncollinear points have at most one equidistant point, since that point must lie on two perpendicular bisectors. Hence the large circle's center is \(O\).

Writing \(R\) for its radius, internal tangency now gives
\[
R-1=2\sqrt3,
\qquad R=1+2\sqrt3.
\]
The 13 unit disks have disjoint interiors because their only intersections are tangencies. Their total area is therefore \(13\pi\), with no overlapping area counted twice. The shaded area is
\[
\pi R^2-13\pi
=\pi\bigl((1+2\sqrt3)^2-13\bigr)
=\boxed{4\pi\sqrt3}.
\]
This is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
